consensus_summary: Swine primarily symbolize uncleanness and spiritual impurity—the unholy, profane, and those who reject or trample sacred things—rooted in Levitical dietary laws and applied in NT texts such as Matthew 7:6 and 2 Peter 2:22; alternatives (Gentiles, apostasy, sensuality, demons, enemies) are treated as extensions of this core.
book_summary: Swine are the unclean beast par excellence, defined by the outward sign of a parted hoof without the inward work of chewing the cud, and identified as the nation outside the covenant that tramples what is holy (pearls, holy city, washed sow).
consensus_core_identification: uncleanness / spiritual impurity (the profane who reject or trample sacred things)
book_core_identification: unclean beast with outward form lacking inward reality; the nation outside the covenant that tramples what is holy
boundary_disagreement: Book elevates the specific legal defect (cloven hoof without cud) and the Gentile/nation-outside-covenant referent (linked via Rev 11:2) to definitional status, whereas consensus keeps general impurity broader and treats the hypocrisy reading and Gentile application as minority or secondary alternatives.
material_contradiction: None; the book retains and builds on the uncleanness core without denying it.
rationale: Both share the Levitical uncleanness foundation and the trampling motif from Matthew 7:6 / 2 Peter 2:22. The book preserves that category but materially narrows its precision and extension by making the partial-cleanness criterion and the covenant-outsider nation the explicit core identification rather than optional elaborations. This is boundary refinement, not core replacement or novelty.
strongest_objection: Consensus ranks the cloven-hoof hypocrisy note and the Gentile/nation reading as secondary or minority, not primary, so the book’s elevation of them may over-specify a broader impurity symbol.
